lesson.title: il y a
lesson.subtitle: 'It has there' = there is / there are — and with a time span, 'ago' (il y a trois ans)

hook.title: Three Tiny Words You Already Own
hook.content: Take il ('it'), y ('there', from Topic 22), and a ('has', from Topic 10) and snap them together: il y a (/il j‿a/). Word for word, it says 'It has there'. In French, that three-word machine does TWO massive jobs: (1) Before a thing or person, it means both 'there is' AND 'there are' (Il y a un café 'There is a café', Il y a deux trains 'There are two trains'). (2) Before a length of time inside a past sentence, it means 'AGO': J'ai visité Paris il y a trois ans ('I visited Paris three years ago')!

footnotes.title: Why il y a never becomes plural *il y ont
footnotes.content: Because il is an impersonal dummy subject ('it') and the nouns after a are direct objects ('it has two trains there'), a stays singular even before a hundred things!

pattern.title: Existence ('There Is/Are') vs. Elapsed Time ('Ago')
pattern.content: Notice the contrast between Topic 20's depuis and Topic 25's il y a with time: J'habite ici depuis trois ans (Present + depuis = 'I have lived here FOR three years', still ongoing) vs. Je suis arrivé il y a trois ans (Passé composé + il y a = 'I arrived three years AGO', completed point in the past)! And to say 'There is not / There are no', wrap n'...pas around y a and collapse the article to de: Il n'y a pas de complication ('There is no complication').
pattern.linguist_note: Spanish hay (ha + y) is the exact historical twin of French il y a, fused into a single word.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: confusing depuis trois ans ('for three years', ongoing) with il y a trois ans ('three years ago', completed). Completed past + il y a = AGO!

exercises.prompt: Match each il y a expression with its meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Il y a un bon restaurant ici
matching_pairs.german: There is a good restaurant here

matching_pairs.english: Il n'y a pas de problème
il y a dix minutes (with past tense)
il y a deux ans (with past tense)

exercises.target_answer: There is a good restaurant here, There are three trains, There is no problem, ten minutes ago, two years ago
exercises.meaning: Il y a un bon restaurant ici, Il y a trois trains, Il n'y a pas de problème, il y a dix minutes (with past tense), il y a deux ans (with past tense)
exercises.explanation: il y a means 'there is/are' before objects, and 'ago' before a time span.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word breakdown of 'Il y a un café ici'?
exercises.german: Il y a un café ici
options: It there has a café here
He there is a café here
exercises.target_answer: It there has a café here
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: It there has a café here

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'She arrived ten minutes ago'?
options: Elle arrive il y a dix minutes
Elle est arrivée depuis dix minutes
Elle est arrivée il y a dix minutes
exercises.target_answer: Elle est arrivée il y a dix minutes
exercises.explanation: A completed past event (est arrivée) + il y a + time span means 'ten minutes ago'.

exercises.idea: there is a good bistro here (use un bon restaurant)
cues: There is → Il y a + a good restaurant here → un bon restaurant ici
exercises.target_answer: Il y a un bon restaurant ici
exercises.meaning: There is a good restaurant here
exercises.explanation: Il y a opens any existence statement.

diagnosis.slip: used Il est instead of Il y a
diagnosis.cue: Use Il y a ('it has there') for 'there is / there are'.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Il n'y a pas de complication
exercises.target_answer: Il n'y a pas de complication
cues: negative existence: Il n'y a pas
exercises.explanation: n' wraps around y a (Il n'y a pas), and une collapses to bare de after negation.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote Il n'y a pas de complication with the negative de.

summary.outcome: Use il y a for both 'there is / there are' and 'ago' (with time spans), and negate it with il n'y a pas de.

use_example.german: Il y a deux ans, il y avait un petit café ici.
use_example.english: Two years ago, there was a small café here.

summary.takeaway: il + y + a ('it there has') means 'there is/are' in space and 'ago' in time.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2501] It Has There): see how il y a leads directly into It Has There.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'I saw this film two years ago' (use J'ai vu ce film):
twist.target_answer: J'ai vu ce film il y a deux ans
twist.explanation: J'ai vu ce film (completed past) + il y a deux ans ('two years ago').

foreshadow.line: Having mastered il y a, look ahead to Topic 26 (The Would-World), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 24 (Reflexives & la Routine) now pays off directly inside il y a: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

il_y_a.english_meaning: there is, there are; ago (with time)
il_y_a.context_phrase: Il y a un bon bistro ici.
il_y_a.context_translation: There is a good bistro here.
il_y_a.etymology_derivation: With a spatial noun it means 'there is/are'; with a time span (il y a trois jours) it means 'three days ago'!

y.context_phrase: Tu vas à Paris ? — Oui, j'y vais.
y.context_translation: Are you going to Paris? — Yes, I'm going there.
y.etymology_derivation: Replaces any place phrase introduced by à, en, dans, or chez.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

a.etymology_derivation: No accent on a ('has') vs grave accent on à ('to/at').

ans.context_translation: I'm thirty years old (I have thirty years).
ans.etymology_derivation: Latin annus — annual, anniversary. Age is something you have in French: j'ai X ans.

semaine.etymology_derivation: Latin septimāna, the seven-morning stretch. English had the same coin: sennight, seven nights — now extinct.

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin pars minuta prima ('first small part' of an hour). Feminine in French.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

complication.etymology_derivation: Two nasals, one rule: con- and -tion both think their N without saying it.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
